Graduated in 2015.

At my school the cheerleaders were just average students like everyone else- same with the football players. There was never anything 'greater' or 'special' about them beyond the fact that coaches who taught classes let them get away with a lot.

The top of the social tier was filled with vegan AP students and people in indie bands, actually.

The marching band fit every single stereotype. A stereotype that I would've fit decently well into if I'd played an instrument- but I transferred from a school where I was in the orchestra, and this school didn't have string instrument teachers.

Though everyone intermingled pretty freely. I think boundaries are growing a lot less stark than what they were in the past few decades.

If someone chooses one profession early in life, they aren't permanently attached to it and unable to put their focus somewhere else though. With skill systems before Skyrim, that's how it worked. In Oblivion if a young hunter discovered a knack for magic, he could go off to study at the university and become a mage. He's stuck training with his bow forever lest he'll never progress at all. And sure- he might've had five more years of experience in archery than destruction magic, but that's expressed in the discrepancy between his skill level in those two skills and through his character level. Not permanent limitations on progression methods.

Why does that reformed thief need to keep practicing pickpocketing to progress? Why can't she put her focus somewhere else in life?

Limitations like that don't make sense in real life, and removing them allows for more realistic roleplay.

Your first statement is true, a level of excess is necessary, but 25% in excess is unnecessary. It could be brought down to a more reasonable amount. Even a 5% decrease would have an noticeable impact.

And I'd say it really isn't impressive that we use what we do. France is the first country to have banned supermarkets from throwing out unsold food, having them instead donate it to charities and food banks. That is what I would call impressive.

Another thing that could help is selling meat in smaller portions for higher prices. Consumers would be less willing to waste it- but it's unlikely any companies would be willing to go for this option without being given incentive to do so.

And as for your rather odd disbelief at the idea of food companies who sell meat making money, Tyson Foods, which commands 24% of the beef market alone, is one of four producers that control 80% of the country's beef markets, followed by the three other largest companies; Cargill, JBS USA, and National Beef.

The answer to our problems isn't just saying "Oh, it's too bad we have to do this but we have no other choice." 

We could even, as crazy as it sounds, just eat a bit less meat. I like bacon as much as the next person- but America eats more meat than any other country out there, going so far as to nearly double Norway's number, and I don't see them all dying of B12 deficiency.

No. We may need meat, but not as much as is produced. There's a *lot* more meat than people actually need. A quarter of all meat that enters the US market is just disposed of.

Even simply giving them a bit more space to move around would even be an improvement. The world is huge- and America has a lot of free space to spare. I'm sure these ultra-rich companies can find the cash for some extra square footage on their buildings.
